title: AI model can uncover unseen health issues in CT scans
key_facts: Penn Medicine researchers developed an AI model called Percival, described in a study in NPJ Digital Medicine, that reads CT scans for disease signs and future health risks beyond the reason the scan was ordered.
Percival was trained on data from the Penn Medicine BioBank (more than 350,000 people); about 400,000 CT scans from roughly 50,000 patients were used to hone it.
It found traces of atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease, and flagged pancreatic cancer, cirrhosis and bacterial pneumonia much more reliably than a similar model, TotalSegmentator.
Percival is still being tested preclinically; developers hope to test it early next year with a view to clinical use.
Code and training model specifications are open source.
Senior author Walter Witschey, associate professor of Radiology at Penn, hopes to elevate 'opportunistic screening'.
Work supported by the NIH Office of the Director and the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering.
quote_evidence: The researchers used roughly 400,000 CT scans from approximately 50,000 patients to hone Percival’s abilities, which are still being tested preclinically.
Percival’s code and training model specifications are open source, which could also help it improve.
why_it_matters_hint: Routine CT scans could be mined for early signs of unrelated disease.
